title: Embeddings & Reranking: Performance & Cost Deep Dive
summary: Deep technical discussion covering embedding vector dimensionality, batching strategies, KV cache relevance, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem deployment considerations for NovaSearch's reranking pipeline. Agreed to run a benchmark: 100k queries against 10M vectors with two index configs and shared results next week.
topics: KV cache and prefix caching relevance
action_items: Priya Kapoor | Produce benchmark plan + config files for: (a) 384-d index with IVF-PQ, (b) 1536-d HNSW with int8 quantized store | 2025-07-17
Sofia Martinez | Share current production traffic distribution, 95p latency requirement, and existing index size (number of docs) | 2025-07-15
Daniel Park | Grant Redwood trial account access to a staging VPC for on-prem style test; provide contact for security onboarding | 2025-07-18
next_steps: Redwood to run two benchmark configs against NovaSearch staging dataset and share CSV of latency/throughput/cost
Schedule follow-up call week of 2025-07-21 to review benchmark results and decide on pilot
Redwood to provide security checklist and VPC peering template for NovaSearch infra team
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-10 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (NovaSearch HoML), Sofia Martinez (NovaSearch BE), Irina Petrov (NovaSearch Infra), Marco Liu (Product)

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[00:05] Daniel: Daniel here.
[00:06] Sofia: Sofia.
[00:07] Irina: Irina.
[00:08] Marco: Marco.
[00:09] Priya: Priya from Redwood, hi.
[00:11] Liam: Great. Quick agenda — we're doing a deep dive on embeddings + reranking perf and unit cost, we'll walk through our recommended benchmarking approach, quantization options, and how that fits with VPC/on-prem constraints.

[00:30] Priya: To start, can you outline your current stack and numbers so we can ground recommendations — docs count, vector dim, latency SLOs, traffic distribution?
[00:38] Daniel: Sure. Prod index is about 10 million docs right now, embeddings are 1536 dims from an off-the-shelf model. Reranking is two-stage: dense retrieval with FAISS and then a cross-encoder on top for top-50 items. 95th percentile for search latency needs to be under 250ms for web queries, but internal dashboards can tolerate up to 500ms. Our QPS at peak is around 200 qps but more bursty.

[01:15] Priya: Awesome. A couple quick clarifications — when you say rerank cross-encoder, is that running per query on CPU or GPU?
[01:22] Daniel: That's CPU for now, it's killing cost and sometimes pushes the latency beyond our targets during spikes. We're evaluating moving the cross-encoder to GPU to speed it up but that's an ops lift.

[01:35] Priya: Thanks. Ok so high-level trade-offs: higher vector dims (e.g., 1536) generally improve retrieval quality but increase index size and ANN search time; lower dims (384) reduce storage and ANN cost and can be 2–4x cheaper, but quality can drop depending on model and task. For reranking cost, you can either (A) keep cross-encoder and optimize placement (GPU + batch), or (B) invest in a stronger two-tower embedding + better index to reduce candidate set size, or (C) use distilled cross-encoder for cheaper re-score.

[02:20] Marco: Distilled cross-encoder? Is that usually acceptable for relevance?
[02:24] Priya: Often yes for many search verticals. There's a small hit on difficult queries, but it can be a good middle ground. We'll provide concrete numbers in the benchmark.

[02:36] Sofia: On embedding dims — we've been worried about dropping 1536 to 384. Wouldn't we lose recall?

[02:41] Priya: Potentially. But it's model-dependent. Some modern encoders trained with contrastive objectives maintain strong retrieval at 384 dims. Also, you can quantize 1536-d vectors (int8, PQ) to reduce storage without full dimensionality reduction. For latency, ANN algorithms like HNSW are sensitive to dim: higher dims increase distance computation time, but with GPU-based search or sharding you can offset.

[03:10] Liam: I want to call out cost math here. If you keep 1536 and don't quantize, 10M vectors is heavy — storage and memory footprint for an in-memory ANN like HNSW could be tens to hundreds of GB depending on indexing params. Quantized IVF-PQ stores can bring that down by 4–8x. But the trade-off is recall/latency.

[03:45] Irina: For our compliance team, we need a VPC/on-prem option. Network egress and peering are big. If we do dedicated Redwood Dedicated or Private, how does that change latency/cost?

[03:55] Liam: With Dedicated you get reserved capacity and predictable throughput — you can pin GPUs for cross-encoder inference and colocate index shards to reduce network hops. Private (VPC) can live in your cloud region with peering or on-prem appliance; egress is minimal because everything is inside your network, but there's an ops overhead for provisioning. We gave a VPC peering template in the pre-call notes — we'll share a more detailed checklist for your infra.

[04:30] Marco: Let's get into batch sizing for embeddings generation — our ingestion pipeline creates 50k new docs a day, and reindexing full dataset isn't frequently done, but we do embeddings at ingest. What's recommended batch behavior?

[04:40] Priya: For embedding generation, batching on the model side is critical. On GPU, batching 128–512 embeds can amortize kernel overhead and push throughput, but increases tail latency per batch. For near-real-time ingest where per-item latency matters, you might batch 16–64. It also depends if you use CPU or GPU. On CPU (AVX optimized) you'd aim for smaller batches because of memory constraints.

[05:15] Sofia: Any hard numbers for per-embed latency?

[05:18] Priya: Rough ballpark — on a single A10/A100 GPU, 1536-d embed generation for a batch of 128 might be ~40–80ms batch latency (so ~0.3–0.6ms per item) depending on model. On CPU it's an order of magnitude higher — tens to hundreds of ms per item. These are rough; we'll include exacts in the benchmark CSV.

[05:42] Daniel: That's surprising — GPU seems very good. So the main cost is inference + index search + cross-encoder rerank. If we move cross-encoder to GPU, we pay for GPU cycles but reduce tail latency. What's Redwood's recommended approach?

[05:56] Priya: For web search with 95p <= 250ms, typical pattern is: embeddings retrieval + cheap re-ranker (distilled) on CPU for most queries; for premium/SLAd customers or very complex queries you can fallback to GPU cross-encoder. Or you can precompute reranks for popular queries. Also, with Redwood's smart routing you can route premium queries to dedicated GPU pool and others to cheaper CPU cluster.

[06:30] Liam: Let's discuss KV cache — note it's more relevant to autoregressive generation. For embeddings and reranking KV is less applicable unless you do cache of recent queries/candidates. We see customers use prefix/KV cache for conversational retrieval augmentation where past contexts are reused; that can reduce token compute but not ANN search cost directly.

[06:55] Sofia: So for our two-stage pipeline, caching top-k results for repeated queries would help. How do you recommend TTLs?

[07:01] Priya: Depends on query stability. For news vertical, short TTL like 1–5 minutes; for product search maybe hours. Cache keys should include query normalization and filters. Redwood supports configurable TTLs and can do prefix-aware invalidation.

[07:20] Daniel: Ok good. Quantization — we want concrete guidance on int8 vs 4-bit vs PQ.

[07:27] Priya: Int8 (linear quantization) often gives a good quality/cost balance, reducing storage by ~2x vs float32. Product quantization (PQ) and OPQ can go further (4–8x), but increase decoding time for exact reconstruct or require asymmetric distance computations in ANN. 4-bit quant (e.g., GPTQ-style) is aggressive and best for model weights; for vectors PQ is usually the go-to. For cross-encoder weights, int8 or 4-bit quantization yields good GPU memory savings but watch for small accuracy drops — we'll measure that.

[08:10] Irina: For on-prem, are there restrictions for quantized indexes? Any special library requirements?

[08:15] Priya: You'll need FAISS or similar with PQ support (we also support Milvus/Weaviate/HNSW integrations). For GPU search we use FAISS-GPU kernels — if on-prem GPU drivers need to be compatible. We'll provide a driver and software checklist.

[08:35] Marco: Let's go over a sample benchmark plan — Daniel you said 10M docs. What configs should Redwood run?

[08:41] Priya: We'll run two main index configs against a 100k-query sample from your traffic: (A) 384-d embedding model with HNSW index tuned for recall@100, little to no quantization; (B) 1536-d embeddings with IVF-PQ (8 bytes per vector effective) + HNSW hybrid for candidates and a quantized cross-encoder on GPU for rerank. We'll capture metrics: qps, 95p and 99p latency for retrieval and rerank, storage footprint, and cost estimate (GPU hours, memory).

[09:15] Daniel: How about batch sizes for rerank on GPU?

[09:18] Priya: For cross-encoder scoring you can batch top-k candidates per query across queries. Batch sizes of 64–256 maximize GPU utilization but increase per-query latency unless you use asynchronous batching with latency SLO-aware timeouts. Redwood supports adaptive batching where we try to keep per-query SLOs while maximizing batch fill.

[09:45] Sofia: There's also question of partial rerank — like re-ranking only top-10 with cross-encoder rather than top-50.

[09:50] Priya: Exactly — that reduces compute linearly. Our benchmarks will include top-10 vs top-50 cost/latency deltas. Often top-10 gives most of the UX gains.

[10:05] Marco: Networking — if we run Private in our VPC, what's the expected network latency between our app and the Redwood runtime?

[10:12] Liam: If peered in same region, sub-ms to low-ms typical. The biggest hits are when data crosses regions or if we fall back to hosted over the public internet. We'll provide a VPC peering template and recommended placement.

[10:30] Irina: Security — we need audit logs and KMS integration.

[10:34] Liam: We support KMS/HSM integration, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and have audit logs. For Private deployments we can enable customer-managed KMS. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and the security checklist as requested.

[11:00] (longer discussion, Priya screen-shares a benchmark design sheet)

[11:10] Priya: On the screen — here's the plan: 100k sampled queries, 10M corpus. We'll run three runs: baseline (1536 float32 HNSW), quantized IVF-PQ 1536, and compressed 384 with HNSW. Metrics: recall@10/50, p95/p99 lat retrieval, rerank CPU vs GPU cost, storage. We'll also run permutations for batch sizes during embedding generation: 16, 64, 256.

[11:40] Daniel: Sounds good. For the cost estimate, can Redwood show unit economics (cost per 1k queries)?

[11:46] Liam: Yes we'll calculate cost per 1k using GPU/CPU pricing and memory overhead assumptions; we'll include amortized index rebuild cost monthly.

[12:00] Marco: Any gotchas for hybrid architectures?

[12:03] Priya: Watch for unbalanced shards — sharding by id or geographic region can create hot shards increasing p99. Also HNSW memory blow-up for high efConstruction parameters. And watch for vector drift when model changes — you may need reindexing. We recommend versioned indexes and can do incremental reindexing to reduce full rebuilds.

[12:30] Sofia: One more on quantization — if we do PQ, how much slower is query-time distance computation?

[12:35] Priya: There's decode overhead but FAISS supports asymmetric distance that computes approximate distances quickly; typical query-time overhead is modest (10–30% slower) compared to full-fp depending on config — again, we'll measure.

[12:50] Daniel: Ok let's recap next actions.
[12:53] Liam: Recap: Redwood will run benchmarks (Priya leads) with configs A/B, share CSV + dashboard, and provide security and VPC templates. NovaSearch will share traffic sample and grant staging access. We'll meet the week of 2025-07-21.

[13:10] Marco: Thanks all.

[13:12] (call ends)
